text: Is objective truth attainable, or is all knowledge inescapably subjective? Few questions have proven as contentious within philosophical discourse. At the core of this debate lies a paradox: the very act of claiming that truth is relative presupposes some fixed standard against which relativity can be measured. Epistemology, the study of knowledge itself, forces us to discern between beliefs that are merely convenient and those that are genuinely coherent. Sceptics argue that human perception is inherently limited, and that what we accept as fact is often little more than a socially constructed fallacy we rationalize to preserve comfort. Others insist that certain truths transcend culture and circumstance altogether, underpinning morality and science alike. Were this dichotomy easily resolved, philosophers would long ago have abandoned the argument. Instead, the debate persists precisely because both positions capture something real: our judgments are shaped by context, yet not every claim is equally valid simply because it is ambiguous or unfalsifiable. Consequently, rather than discrediting either extreme outright, many contemporary thinkers propose a middle path, one that acknowledges subjectivity without collapsing into total skepticism.

questions.question: What is the central philosophical question explored in the passage?
options: Whether religion is more valid than science
Whether objective truth exists or all knowledge is subjective
How language shapes personal identity
Whether ethics should be taught in schools

questions.question: According to the passage, what paradox arises from claiming truth is relative?
options: It requires no evidence at all
It presupposes a fixed standard by which relativity itself is judged
It proves that all beliefs are equally false
It eliminates the need for epistemology

questions.question: What can be inferred about the "middle path" mentioned at the end?
options: It rejects both skepticism and belief in transcendent truth entirely
It attempts to balance the recognition of subjectivity with belief in some valid, more objective claims
It argues that all truths are purely cultural constructs
It dismisses the value of philosophical discourse

questions.question: How does the passage describe skeptics' view of accepted facts?
options: As objective and unquestionable
As often a socially constructed fallacy people rationalize
As entirely based on scientific proof
As irrelevant to epistemology

questions.question: What best describes the author's purpose in this passage?
options: To argue decisively that relativism is correct
To present a balanced, analytical examination of a longstanding philosophical debate
To ridicule philosophers for wasting time on trivial questions
To provide a historical timeline of epistemology

questions.question: Why does the debate over truth persist, according to the passage?
options: Because philosophers have never seriously considered it
Because both the subjective and transcendent positions capture some valid insight
Because governments prevent resolution
Because there is no real disagreement among thinkers
